courses.title: 11. Debug and test native desktop behavior
courses.summary: Test portable C++ rules, inspect the running XAML tree, and distinguish build evidence from UI evidence.

lessons.title: Test each boundary where it can fail
paragraphs: A task app has at least three useful test layers: portable title rules, the window’s interaction flow and the installed application. Console tests can exercise rules quickly without starting WinUI. UI tests then verify that controls call those rules correctly and render their outcomes.

Keep TaskRules.h independent of WinUI so the same input cases can run with a standard C++ compiler. The sample tests trimming, empty input, control characters and both sides of the length boundary. Testing a separately reimplemented rule would not verify the rule the window actually uses.
lessons.example:
Portable rule → deterministic input/output tests
Window → native input, focus and visible state
Package → install, launch, update and data retention
lessons.pitfall: A green portable test run cannot prove that XAML names or event wiring are correct.

question.prompt: What do the portable tests verify?

options.text: The MSIX installer on every machine

question.explanation: Each test layer has a specific scope of evidence.

lessons.title: Test edges and rejected transactions
paragraphs: The important title cases are not just Read XAML. Test an empty string, tabs and spaces, embedded newlines, 80 units and 81 units, plus ordinary non-ASCII text. For each rejection check that accepted state did not change.

A capstone regression should also test saving, closing, reloading and recovering from invalid storage. Write down exact expected values before running. This keeps tests from simply repeating whatever the implementation happened to return.
lessons.example:
Length 80 → accepted
Length 81 → rejected
Spaces only → rejected
Padded valid text → trimmed and accepted
lessons.pitfall: Only testing happy-path titles misses the conditions most likely to damage a document or confuse a user.

question.prompt: Which pair tests the length boundary?
question.explanation: Values on opposite sides of the rule catch off-by-one errors.

lessons.title: Use the debugger to locate the faulty layer
paragraphs: Set a breakpoint at the handler boundary and inspect the captured title, validation result and collection size. If the handler never runs, compare the XAML event name with the C++ declaration and definition. If it runs with the wrong text, inspect the named input accessor and state ownership.

Use Visual Studio’s available XAML inspection tools to examine the running object tree and layout bounds. If a source name is missing during compilation, check x:Class, namespace and generated inputs before manually editing a generated header. First failure evidence usually narrows the problem more than repeated clean builds.
lessons.example:
Handler reached? → input correct? → rule result correct?
→ collection changed? → view notified? → layout visible?
lessons.pitfall: Repeated rebuilds cannot fix a logical error in a handler that is already compiling and running.

question.prompt: The handler is never reached. What should you inspect first?

options.text: The XAML event hookup and matching method

question.explanation: Start at the earliest broken boundary in the action chain.

lessons.title: Report what actually ran
paragraphs: Record the OS, architecture, configuration and dependency versions with native results. A browser can display these source files and verify course assessments, but it cannot compile or launch WinUI here. Separate native launch results from portable tests and source structure checks.

Use a small regression matrix for Add, invalid Add, remove selection, cancel, file failure and close-during-work. Re-run the cases affected by a code change. Release performance measurements should come from the actual Release executable with its environment stated, not from the lesson’s timer demonstration.
lessons.example:
Evidence: toolchain + input + expected result + observed result
Mark unexecuted Windows checks as pending, never as passed.
lessons.pitfall: A production build of this website is not a build of its downloadable C++ WinUI examples.

question.prompt: What can a browser source-view check establish?

options.text: That the intended source is displayed and downloaded

question.explanation: Native execution needs a Windows environment and separate observation.

steps: Compile and run TaskRules.test.cpp using the README’s console command.
Build the WinUI sample and inspect the validation result in the debugger.
Change the 80-unit rule deliberately, rerun the boundary tests, then restore it.
Record which checks ran on Windows and which only tested portable C++.
courses.expected: The portable suite reports its counted checks. The native window presents matching validation outcomes; website tests alone do not establish a Windows launch.

challenge.task: Write a short regression report for the task notebook covering domain, UI and packaging layers.
acceptance: Include a failing case before its fix.
Record the exact native toolchain.
Label any unexecuted check as pending.

questions.prompt: A test copies the validation algorithm into another function. What is the weakness?

options.text: It replaces the need for assertions
It may pass while the shipped rule is broken

questions.explanation: Tests should exercise the same rule the window calls.

questions.prompt: A rejected title still increments the task count. Which assertion catches it?

options.text: Accepted state remains unchanged after invalid input

questions.explanation: A rejection test must inspect state as well as error text.

questions.prompt: The handler runs and the vector changes, but the list does not. Where next?
questions.explanation: The earliest known good boundaries narrow the remaining fault.

questions.prompt: Only website tests ran on macOS. Which claim is accurate?

options.text: Course behavior was tested; WinUI native launch remains unverified
All Windows desktop samples passed native launch

questions.explanation: Report the environment and scope of actual execution.

questions.prompt: What should accompany a Release timing claim?

options.text: The duration of a teaching delay
Measured native results and a stated environment

questions.explanation: Performance claims need actual measurements of the target executable.

courses.title: 12. Package, install and update the app
courses.summary: Understand MSIX identity, runtime dependencies and architecture, then test the installed application beyond Visual Studio.

lessons.title: Separate package identity from executable name
paragraphs: MSIX packaging describes the application’s identity, publisher, version, assets and deployment behavior. The executable filename is only one part of that artifact. Start from the packaged C++ template so generated assets and build settings form a coherent baseline.

Keep identity stable when testing an update that should retain the same application data. A differently named package may install alongside the old one instead of replacing it. Record the manifest identity and version with your test evidence so you know which app was launched.
lessons.example:
Record: identity name, publisher, version, target architecture
Then test installation and launch from the installed app entry.
lessons.pitfall: Renaming the EXE does not by itself define a correct package identity or update path.

question.prompt: What identifies an MSIX application beyond its EXE name?

options.text: Package metadata including identity and publisher

question.explanation: Deployment identity is defined by the package contract.

lessons.title: Choose a dependency strategy deliberately
paragraphs: Framework-dependent deployment relies on an appropriate installed Windows App SDK runtime. Self-contained deployment includes runtime components with the app at a size and servicing cost. Packaging choice and runtime-dependency choice are related but are not the same setting.

Follow the deployment guidance for the exact stable SDK version selected by your template. Do not copy a partial property list and assume it covers signing, initialization and dependencies for every packaged or unpackaged scenario. This path keeps its sample project packaged; unpackaged deployment is a later extension to validate separately.
lessons.example:
Framework-dependent: app + required runtime installation
Self-contained: app includes runtime components
Both still need architecture and deployment validation.
lessons.pitfall: A framework-dependent executable may work on a developer PC only because the runtime is already installed there.

question.prompt: Why test on a machine without development tools?
question.explanation: The development environment can hide missing runtime prerequisites.

lessons.title: Treat architecture and trust as release inputs
paragraphs: Build the architecture you intend to ship and test it on a compatible Windows machine. Match dependent native libraries to that architecture. Debug and Release are separate configurations; verify the installed Release build rather than assuming Debug launch proves a release artifact.

A sideloaded package needs an appropriate signing and trust setup. A development certificate is a local testing tool, not a universal distribution identity. Keep signing credentials outside source downloads and use the documented distribution process for your audience. The course provides a release checklist, not a signed installer.
lessons.example:
Source pack ≠ built executable ≠ signed MSIX
Verify each artifact separately.
lessons.pitfall: Shipping a private signing key inside an example archive is not a setup shortcut.

question.prompt: Does the lesson source archive contain a signed installer?

options.text: No; the learner builds and packages it on Windows
Yes; a .cpp file is an MSIX
Only if downloaded in dark mode

question.explanation: Source files still require a native build and a deployment process.

lessons.title: Exercise install, update and data retention
paragraphs: Create a task with the installed app, save it, close the process and reopen from the Start menu. Then build an update with the same intended identity and a higher package version, install it and inspect the saved task. Also test a fresh installation with no pre-existing data.

Document uninstall behavior, supported OS requirements and the runtime strategy for the selected SDK. A working update on one machine is local evidence, not certification of every Windows device. Keep a recovery copy of test data when deliberately exercising failure paths.
lessons.example:
Fresh install → launch → save → restart
Update same identity → launch → verify prior data
Separate test: uninstall behavior
lessons.pitfall: Launching only through F5 misses installed-app activation and dependency problems.

question.prompt: Which launch path belongs in a deployment test?

options.text: The installed app entry outside Visual Studio

question.explanation: Users launch an installed artifact, so test that path.

steps: Build the downloadable package-ready sample in the C++ packaged template.
Record identity, SDK version, architecture and dependency strategy.
Produce and install a Release package using the template’s packaging workflow.
Launch outside Visual Studio and run the release checklist on a separate test environment.
courses.expected: The sample shows its release-check prompt after launch. Installation, signing, runtime availability and update behavior require actual Windows verification and are not supplied by the source archive.

challenge.task: Prepare an install-and-update report for the capstone with a documented runtime strategy.
acceptance: Launch the installed Release app outside the IDE.
Verify an update retains the intended saved data.
Keep private signing material out of the source pack.

questions.prompt: An update installs as a second app. What should you compare?
questions.explanation: Different identities can result in separate installations.

questions.prompt: The EXE works only on the developer PC. What is a likely deployment gap?

options.text: An undeclared or missing runtime dependency

questions.explanation: A development machine may already contain required components.

questions.prompt: Does packaged always mean self-contained?

options.text: No; packaging and runtime strategy are distinct choices

questions.explanation: MSIX and dependency inclusion address different concerns.

questions.prompt: What should a shared source archive exclude?
questions.explanation: Signing secrets are not source dependencies for learners.

questions.prompt: F5 works. What deployment evidence is still missing?

options.text: Installed Release launch and dependency/update checks
Any need to test outside the IDE

questions.explanation: Debug launch does not cover installed distribution behavior.

sources.title: Package a desktop app with single-project MSIX

courses.title: 13. Ship a C++ task notebook
courses.summary: Combine validation, an observable list, safe selection, asynchronous local JSON saving and a complete desktop verification plan.

lessons.title: Define a small complete application
paragraphs: The capstone accepts up to 100 task titles, rejects invalid entries, removes a selected task, and explicitly saves or loads a versioned document in the packaged app’s local data folder. The title rule is the same portable C++ header used earlier. A status line distinguishes an unsaved edit from a completed save.

This is intentionally a small task notebook: titles are ordered strings with no login, cloud sync, scheduling or collaborative edits. That scope lets you finish an understandable vertical slice. Starting a fresh process does not automatically load data; choose Load saved to make the disk boundary visible.
lessons.example:
Add → validate → append → unsaved
Remove selected → bounds check → remove → unsaved
Save → snapshot → async write → saved status
lessons.pitfall: Calling an in-memory list saved before the file operation succeeds gives users false confidence.

question.prompt: When may the capstone report a successful save?
question.explanation: Visible success must follow the operation it describes.

lessons.title: Version and validate the saved document
paragraphs: The file contains a version number and a tasks array. JSON preserves quotes and non-ASCII titles through structured encoding. On load, enforce a byte limit, the expected schema version, the task-count limit, string item types and the same title rule before replacing the current collection.

Build a temporary vector from the entire document first. If one item is invalid, retain the current list and show an error. Do not accept a malformed file halfway and silently throw away the learner’s good tasks. The current implementation has one schema version; a future migration needs an explicit tested conversion.
lessons.example: {"version":1,"tasks":["Read XAML","Test keyboard input"]}
lessons.pitfall: A parseable JSON object is not necessarily a valid task document.

question.prompt: What should happen when the third loaded item is invalid?

options.text: Reject the document and retain the current list
Keep only its first two items silently

question.explanation: Validate the complete candidate before committing it.

lessons.title: Snapshot state and serialize operations
paragraphs: The window serializes the current accepted collection into a local string before the first await. It locks editing while a save or load is pending, avoiding overlap and making the result’s ownership easy to explain. StorageFile and FileIO perform the asynchronous local write; the UI does not call blocking get.

Saving replaces the lesson’s named local file. This is a teaching persistence path, not a crash-proof transactional database: a power loss or failing replacement can still require recovery. Loading asks before replacing current tasks. Cancel preserves the current list, and a closed-window guard prevents late control updates.
lessons.example:
Snapshot JSON → mark busy → await local write
Success → show Saved
Failure → preserve in-memory tasks, show error, allow retry
lessons.pitfall: Serializing controls after an await can save a different state from the one that started the operation.

question.prompt: Why snapshot before awaiting the write?

options.text: To save a defined accepted state

question.explanation: Each operation needs clear ownership of its input data.

lessons.title: Demonstrate the whole desktop flow
paragraphs: Add two tasks, attempt an invalid third, remove one selection, save, close, relaunch and load. Then cancel a replacement and try loading an invalid document in a disposable app-data test environment. Confirm that good in-memory tasks survive failures and that the status matches the real outcome.

Run the portable tests, test narrow and large-text layouts, check keyboard behavior, and produce an installed Release build using the packaging course. These are separate evidence categories. The downloadable pack supplies complete MainWindow replacement files and portable rules, while Windows compilation, native UI behavior and MSIX distribution remain tasks for your Windows toolchain.
lessons.example:
Acceptance: valid edits + rejected edits + save/restart/load
Recovery: canceled replacement + invalid document + failed write
Release: keyboard + resize + installed launch
lessons.pitfall: A screenshot of two tasks does not demonstrate persistence, recovery or installed-app behavior.

question.prompt: Which sequence proves persistence beyond process memory?

options.text: Save, close, relaunch, then load and compare

question.explanation: A new process must recover the accepted data from storage.

steps: Build the pack in VoltQuestDesktop and add Read XAML and Test keyboard input.
Reject a blank title, select one task and remove it; save the remaining list.
Close and relaunch, choose Load saved and confirm replacement; compare the exact title.
Repeat with canceled replacement, invalid storage in a disposable test profile, keyboard input and an installed Release build.
courses.expected: The accepted list survives save → close → relaunch → explicit load. Invalid titles or documents and canceled replacement preserve accepted state; failures report an error without claiming a successful save.

challenge.task: Extend the notebook with completion state and a tested version-1-to-version-2 document migration.
acceptance: Provide complete C++/WinRT and XAML changes.
Retain old title-only documents through a tested migration.
Cover save/reload, invalid import and selection bounds.
Record native toolchain, accessibility and installation evidence; mark anything untested.

questions.prompt: Save is clicked but FileIO later fails. Which status is correct?

options.text: An error with in-memory tasks retained

questions.explanation: An attempted write is not a completed save.

questions.prompt: A valid JSON object has version 99. What should version 1 do?

options.text: Delete the version and load everything
Reject the unsupported schema without replacing tasks

questions.explanation: Version compatibility needs an explicit migration or rejection policy.

questions.prompt: Why build a candidate vector before replacing ItemsSource data?

options.text: To validate the whole document before committing

questions.explanation: Atomic acceptance preserves the old valid state when any candidate item fails.

questions.prompt: What is a stated limitation of this teaching save path?

options.text: It is not a crash-proof transactional database
It compiles C++ in the browser

questions.explanation: Replacement and filesystem failures still require a documented recovery strategy.

questions.prompt: Which evidence completes the native task notebook flow?

options.text: Installed launch plus edits, rejection and save/restart/load checks

questions.explanation: The app’s real behavior spans interaction, persistence and deployment.
